messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin, a 60‑year‑old European warehouse worker, returned to civilian life after twenty years in the Army. On the day of the incident, a sudden artillery burst hit the forward observation post where he was standing, killing four of his squad while he miraculously escaped uninjured. Years later, the weight of having survived when others did not gnawed at him. He had come to believe that the world was inherently dangerous and that his own life had lost its meaning. Because of this conviction, Martin began to keep a strict routine of avoidance: he avoided the exact building he had occupied during the attack, shunned any clothing that resembled his former uniform, and made a deliberate effort not to think about the event, even in the quiet of his apartment. These appraisals did not remain abstract; when Martin recalled the artillery blast, he was struck by an immediate wave of guilt for having survived, and the memory unfolded with a terrifying fidelity that felt almost identical to the heat of the blast itself. He could not find words to describe the scene, as if the language had been taken out of his grasp, and the terror that accompanied the recollection was as intense as the moment itself. The conviction that the world was dangerous amplified this vividness, making each flashback feel like a warning that the safety he had once known was forever gone. Each time the terrifying memory resurfaced, Martin would instinctively retreat from the place that had become a symbol of his loss. The warehouse where he now worked, with its humming conveyors and echoing metal, felt eerily similar to the observation post, so he began arriving early to avoid the crowds and to keep a short shift whenever possible. He also replaced his dark olive field jacket with a bright orange safety vest, believing that the more distinct his clothing was from the uniform that now haunted his thoughts, the safer he would feel. The act of turning away from any thoughts of that night was so compelling that he would often skip his night shift to avoid the lull when his mind might wander into the past. The vividness of the recollection only deepened Martin’s sense that the world had irrevocably changed. Each flashback served as a reminder that he could never return to the person he had been before, reinforcing his feeling of identity loss. The terror that accompanied the memory made him believe that danger lurked not just in distant places but in the everyday routine of the warehouse, a place he had once trusted. He started to fear that his own judgment was unreliable, that he could not rely on his senses to keep him safe, and that the safety he had once known was a fleeting illusion. By the time Martin began consulting a therapist, his avoidance had become so pervasive that even the sound of the loading dock’s alarm reminded him of the artillery that had once erupted in his mind. His habit of staying away from the warehouse at peak times and of avoiding any clothing reminiscent of his former uniform kept him constantly on edge, reinforcing the belief that he was living in a world that could snap into danger at any moment. The more he sidestepped the place that had defined the trauma, the more he convinced himself that survival had been a betrayal, that the only way to survive was to remain detached from the memories that might surface. In the end, the avoidance that once felt like protection had become a prison that amplified every ounce of guilt and fear he carried. His fear that the relentless avoidance would erase the person he loved most—himself and his partner—prompted him to step into therapy, hoping to reclaim a sense of safety and identity.
